studyNotes.title: How Cells Respond to Stress
studyNotes.summary: Cell injury begins when stress exceeds adaptive capacity.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Reversible injury
Early ATP loss disrupts ion gradients, producing cellular swelling and membrane blebs. Recovery is possible while mitochondria and membranes remain functional.

### Irreversible injury
Severe mitochondrial dysfunction and membrane failure prevent restoration of homeostasis and lead to cell death.

### Clinical reasoning
Relate the duration of the insult to the biopsy: swelling and blebs with preserved membranes can recover, while membrane rupture and mitochondrial failure point to irreversible injury.
keyPoints: Cell swelling signals disturbed ion balance; membrane rupture signals severe injury.
Irreversible injury: Severe mitochondrial dysfunction and membrane failure prevent restoration of homeostasis and lead to cell death.
Relate the duration of the insult to the biopsy: swelling and blebs with preserved membranes can recover, while membrane rupture and mitochondrial failure point to irreversible injury.
mnemonics: Stress response: adapt, recover, or die.

studyNotes.title: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis
studyNotes.summary: Apoptosis and necrosis differ in control, morphology, and inflammatory effect.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Apoptosis
A regulated caspase program produces cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, and membrane-bound bodies that are cleared by phagocytes.

### Necrosis
Severe injury causes swelling and membrane rupture, releasing intracellular contents that recruit inflammation.

### Clinical reasoning
Compare cell size, membrane integrity, nuclear change, and inflammation. Apoptosis typically packages cell fragments for quiet clearance; necrosis releases contents and provokes inflammation.
keyPoints: Caspases drive apoptosis; membrane failure defines necrotic injury.
Necrosis: Severe injury causes swelling and membrane rupture, releasing intracellular contents that recruit inflammation.

studyNotes.title: Adaptive Changes and Their Limits
studyNotes.summary: Adaptation can preserve cell survival but may trade normal function for stress tolerance.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Common adaptations
Hypertrophy enlarges cells, hyperplasia increases cell number, atrophy reduces cellular mass, and metaplasia changes differentiated cell type.

### Clinical interpretation
These responses may regress when the cause ends. Persistent stress can impair function and promote dysplasia or irreversible injury.

### Clinical reasoning
Name the adaptive pattern before judging its consequence: increased workload can enlarge cells, hormonal signals can increase cell number, and persistent metaplasia may create a setting for dysplasia.
keyPoints: Metaplasia is a change in cell type; dysplasia is disordered maturation.
Clinical interpretation: These responses may regress when the cause ends.

studyNotes.title: Acute Inflammation: From Signal to Cell
studyNotes.summary: Acute inflammation rapidly recruits cells and plasma proteins to contain injury.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Vascular changes
Vasodilation increases flow, while endothelial permeability allows protein-rich fluid to enter tissue.

### Leukocyte recruitment
Selectins mediate rolling, integrins support firm adhesion, and chemotactic signals guide leukocytes through tissue. Neutrophils often predominate early.

### Clinical reasoning
Link redness and warmth to vasodilation, and protein-rich swelling to increased permeability; then use the timing and dominant leukocyte to distinguish an acute response from a later phase.
keyPoints: Vasodilation causes warmth and redness; permeability causes protein-rich edema.
Leukocyte recruitment: Selectins mediate rolling, integrins support firm adhesion, and chemotactic signals guide leukocytes through tissue.

mnemonics: Roll, adhere, cross, follow the gradient.

studyNotes.title: Chronic Inflammation and Granulomas
studyNotes.summary: Chronic inflammation can combine persistent injury with attempted repair.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Cell populations
Macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells sustain mediator release and tissue remodeling.

### Granulomatous pattern
Epithelioid macrophages and giant cells organize around persistent material. This pattern narrows possibilities but does not establish a specific cause by itself.

### Clinical reasoning
A granuloma is an organized macrophage response to a persistent stimulus. Interpret it with exposure history, tissue site, and organism testing rather than treating the pattern alone as a diagnosis.
keyPoints: Persistent stimuli can drive both tissue destruction and fibrosis.
Granulomatous pattern: Epithelioid macrophages and giant cells organize around persistent material.

mnemonics: Chronic means ongoing injury plus repair.

studyNotes.title: Wound Healing and Scar Formation
studyNotes.summary: Healing restores continuity, but the result may not reproduce original tissue architecture.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Repair phases
Inflammation clears debris, granulation tissue supplies capillaries and fibroblasts, and collagen remodels over time.

### Wound geometry
Closely opposed edges usually heal with less granulation and a smaller scar than wounds with major tissue loss.

### Clinical reasoning
Assess healing by tissue loss, blood supply, infection, and edge approximation. These factors help explain whether repair restores architecture or leaves a larger scar.
